title: Direct identifiability from rich biometric and location telemetry disclosed by the wearer
description: By wearing and using the device, the wearer discloses heart-rate patterns, GPS position, timestamps, and activity data to the wearable. This combination can directly identify or single out the individual, especially when location traces reveal home/work or habitual routines.
assumptions: The wearable or its operator can associate incoming telemetry with a device/account or otherwise distinguish one wearer from others.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types but not the detailed subtree for identifiability.

title: Linkability of multiple observations about the same wearer through continuous telemetry sharing
description: Continuous submission of sensor telemetry lets the recipient correlate many events over time as belonging to the same wearer. Repeated heart-rate, step-count, GPS, and timestamp data can be linked into a persistent behavioral profile.
assumptions: The wearable maintains a persistent device identifier, account, or stable telemetry pattern enabling correlation over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the exact LINDDUN Pro subtree node for linkability was not provided in the retrieved context.

title: Linkability via stable transmission metadata on the telemetry flow
description: Even aside from payload contents, the telemetry flow may expose stable communication metadata such as device identifiers, network addresses, timing, and transmission frequency. These can allow linking multiple transmissions to the same wearer/device.
assumptions: The flow carries or is accompanied by stable identifiers or observable timing/network metadata.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree node is approximate.

title: Identifiability from location-time patterns in transit
description: GPS coordinates combined with timestamps in the transmitted telemetry can identify the wearer by revealing unique mobility patterns, home/work locations, or visits to distinctive places, even if explicit names are absent.
assumptions: An observer of the flow or intermediary can access payload data or sufficiently detailed metadata.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree node is approximate.

title: Detectability of sensitive states by the wearable upon receipt of telemetry
description: Once the wearable receives continuous heart-rate, activity, and location data, it can detect sensitive conditions or events such as sleep/wake cycles, exercise habits, presence at specific places, or possible health-related episodes.
assumptions: The wearable processes or stores the telemetry in a way that enables inference of states or events.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort because the detailed detectability subtree was not included in the retrieved context.

title: Unawareness of the extent of continuous sensing and inference by the wearable
description: The wearer may not fully understand that continuous use causes ongoing capture of heart rate, steps, GPS position, and timestamps, nor the extent of profiling and inference the wearable can perform from that data.
assumptions: Not all sensing, retention, or inference behavior is made salient to the wearer at the moment of collection.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree node is approximate.

title: Non-compliance risk if the wearable collects more telemetry than necessary or without valid transparency/consent basis
description: Continuous collection of biometric, activity, location, and timestamp data may exceed what is necessary for a stated purpose, or may occur without sufficiently specific notice, consent, or other lawful basis, creating a privacy non-compliance threat at the receiving process.
assumptions: Applicable law/policy requires purpose limitation, data minimization, transparency, consent, or another lawful basis for this telemetry collection.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree node is approximate and depends on the applicable legal/policy regime.

title: Excessive disclosure of detailed activity and location data by the wearable
description: The wearable shares exercise sessions, GPS traces, device identifier, and timestamps with the companion app. If all fields are sent by default when only a subset is needed for the app feature being used, the source causes avoidable disclosure of personal data, especially precise location and temporal patterns.
assumptions: Assumes the companion app does not strictly require every synced field at full precision for all use cases.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality concepts; exact subnode may differ in the canonical tree.

title: Identification through device identifier and unique sensor batch metadata in transit
description: The flow contains a device id together with timestamps and activity/GPS data. Even if the user is not explicitly named, these attributes can single out the individual device owner and make the data attributable to a specific person.
assumptions: Assumes the device id is stable or otherwise linkable to an account or person.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree subnode is inferred from general LINDDUN identification guidance.

title: Linkability of multiple sync events via persistent identifiers and recurring patterns
description: Repeated syncs carrying the same device id plus timestamps, exercise characteristics, and GPS traces allow separate batches to be linked to the same user over time. This enables reconstruction of routines, habits, and longitudinal profiles across sessions.
assumptions: Assumes the identifier or behavioral pattern remains sufficiently stable across syncs.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode id is best-effort; applicability of linkability is strong.

title: Detectability of sensitive events from traffic timing and payload characteristics
description: Even without reading full contents, the existence, timing, size, and frequency of sync batches can reveal that the user exercised, traveled, or visited locations at particular times. This makes sensitive behavior detectable from the flow itself.
assumptions: Assumes an observer can access network metadata or local communication metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; threat is grounded in metadata-based detectability.

title: Over-collection and retention of raw GPS traces and session history by the companion app
description: On receipt, the companion app may store or further process raw GPS traces, timestamps, and device identifiers beyond what is necessary for immediate synchronization or user-facing functionality. This creates avoidable disclosure at the destination through unnecessary receipt, storage, or secondary use.
assumptions: Assumes the app persists or repurposes the synced raw data rather than minimizing, aggregating, or promptly deleting it.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode id is inferred from destination-side disclosure/processing concepts rather than retrieved text.

title: Unawareness of the scope and sensitivity of data synchronized into the app
description: Users may not realize that precise GPS traces, timestamps, and stable device identifiers are being imported and potentially retained by the companion app. If the app does not clearly communicate this sync scope, users can be unaware of the privacy impact.
assumptions: Assumes the app's notices or UI do not clearly explain the categories, precision, and retention of synced data.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode id is approximate; threat applicability depends on the app's transparency mechanisms.

title: Insufficient user control over synchronization of location and activity data
description: If the companion app automatically ingests all sensor batches without granular controls, the user may be unable to prevent syncing of GPS traces, timestamps, or identifiers, or to choose lower precision/limited sharing. This reduces intervenability over personal data processing.
assumptions: Assumes there are limited or no per-data-type sync controls, pause options, or deletion controls in the app.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode id is best-effort based on non-compliance/intervenability concepts in LINDDUN Pro.

title: User may be unaware of the privacy implications of entering sensitive health data
description: The wearer manually enters calorie intake, meals, and weight into the app. These entries are health- and lifestyle-related personal data, and the act of sharing them can create an unawareness threat if the user does not understand what data are being collected, how detailed they are, or how they may later be used, combined, or retained by the system.
assumptions: Assumes the app may not provide sufficiently clear, timely notice at the point of data entry about collection, downstream use, retention, or sharing.

title: Companion app can detect sensitive health and lifestyle patterns from manual entries
description: On receipt of meal, calorie, and weight entries, the companion app can infer diet habits, weight trends, possible health conditions, and behavior patterns. This creates a detectability/discoverability risk because highly sensitive attributes become apparent from the submitted data.
assumptions: Assumes the app stores or processes the entries in a way that makes such patterns observable within the system or to authorized operators/components.
uncertainty_note: Tree node citation is approximate because the exact detectability subtree node for inference from submitted content was not provided in the retrieved context.

title: Manual nutrition and weight entries can be linked to the wearer profile
description: The destination process receives repeated food, calorie, and weight records from the same user account/device context. These records can be linked over time to the same wearer profile, enabling longitudinal profiling of habits and health-related behavior.
assumptions: Assumes the app associates entries with an account, device identifier, or persistent session.
uncertainty_note: Exact linkability subtree node is selected by best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the relevant L threat-tree excerpt.

title: Manual entries may identify the wearer through unique dietary or weight patterns
description: Even if explicit identifiers are minimized, combinations of meal logs, calorie patterns, timestamps, and weight history may be sufficiently distinctive to identify or single out the wearer when combined with account context or other available data.
assumptions: Assumes the app or related systems maintain auxiliary data that can be combined with these entries.
uncertainty_note: Exact identifiability subtree node is approximate; applicability depends on what auxiliary identifiers or contextual data the app holds.

title: Collection of detailed meal and weight data may exceed what is necessary for the app's purpose
description: The companion app may receive granular meal descriptions, calorie intake, and weight entries that are more detailed than necessary for the stated functionality, creating a non-compliance risk with data minimization or purpose limitation obligations.
assumptions: Assumes the app's stated purpose could be fulfilled with less granular or less frequent data than what is collected through this flow.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on the actual declared purposes, legal basis, and retention/configuration choices, which are not provided.

title: The app may be unable to demonstrate valid user submission context or consent expectations
description: If the companion app does not record the context in which the wearer submitted meal and weight data—such as notices shown, choices made, or timestamps—it may later be difficult to resolve disputes about what the user knowingly provided or agreed to regarding processing.
assumptions: Assumes the system relies on user agreement, notice, or contextual permissions for this category of data processing.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation applicability is moderate rather than certain because the scenario does not explicitly mention disputes, consent capture, or audit logging.

title: App writes more health data than necessary to the store
description: The mobile app may disclose excessive personal health data to the health log store by persisting detailed calorie intake, weight history, and exercise-session records beyond what is strictly needed for the app's stated functionality. This creates an avoidable disclosure at the moment of sharing from P2 to DS1.
assumptions: Assumes some logged fields, granularity, or retention-related attributes are not strictly necessary for the intended service.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is based on best judgement for excessive/avoidable disclosure; exact node label may vary by LINDDUN Pro catalog version.

title: Health log store retains and exposes detailed sensitive history
description: On receipt, the health log store may process or retain detailed health logs in a way that unnecessarily discloses sensitive personal data, including longitudinal weight history and exercise patterns. Centralized storage of this sensitive history increases the privacy impact if the store is broadly accessible internally or retained longer than necessary.
assumptions: Assumes DS1 stores raw or fine-grained historical records and that retention/access controls may exceed strict necessity.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node may differ depending on whether the catalog distinguishes storage, retention, or secondary disclosure explicitly.

title: Health-log transmission can link records to the same user over time
description: Because repeated writes of calorie intake, weight history, and exercise sessions traverse the same app-to-store flow, the transmitted content and associated metadata can enable linking multiple events and records to the same individual over time, revealing behavioral and health patterns.
assumptions: Assumes the flow carries stable identifiers, account/session metadata, device identifiers, or otherwise consistent context enabling correlation across submissions.
uncertainty_note: Specific node id is best-effort; applicability depends on whether stable identifiers or correlatable metadata are present on DF4.

title: Health-log writes may identify the user through content or metadata
description: The data in transit may directly identify the user, or permit identification when combined with metadata such as account identifiers, device identifiers, timestamps, or distinctive health patterns. Even if explicit identifiers are absent, detailed weight and exercise histories can be identifying in context.
assumptions: Assumes DF4 includes direct identifiers or quasi-identifiers, or that the health-log content is sufficiently distinctive to support identification.
uncertainty_note: Node id is approximate; identification may arise from direct identifiers or from inference using quasi-identifiers.

title: Stored health logs may be used for purposes beyond the user's expectation
description: Once written to the health log store, the detailed health records could be used for analytics, profiling, recommendations, or other secondary purposes not expected by the user when entering the data. This creates a detectability/unawareness concern because the user may not understand how their sensitive logs are processed after storage.
assumptions: Assumes downstream uses of DS1 data are not fully transparent to users at collection time.
uncertainty_note: This is included only insofar as the flow description suggests storage without clarifying user visibility into subsequent uses; exact U-node may vary by catalog version.

title: App may collect and store health logs without sufficiently specific consent or legal basis
description: Writing calorie intake, weight history, and exercise-session data to persistent storage may occur without consent or another valid legal basis that is sufficiently specific for this sensitive personal data. The privacy threat arises at the source when P2 initiates the transfer to storage despite potentially inadequate permission or notice.
assumptions: Assumes these health-related logs qualify as sensitive personal data in the applicable jurisdiction and that consent/legal basis management is relevant to this processing.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on jurisdiction, product context, and whether another lawful basis besides consent exists.

title: Excessive collection of precise location traces by the app
description: The companion mobile app writes GPS traces with timestamps to the history store. Precise, timestamped location history is highly sensitive personal data and may exceed what is strictly necessary for the app's purpose if continuous or high-resolution collection is enabled by default or without granular controls.
assumptions: Assumes the app may collect/store continuous or fine-grained location history rather than only the minimum data needed for the user-facing feature.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected as best-fit for avoidable explicit disclosure/collection under data disclosure; exact node wording may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Stored location history enables long-term linkability of user activities
description: By receiving and storing timestamped GPS traces, the location history store can accumulate records that are trivially linkable to the same device/account over time, allowing reconstruction of routines, visits, and movement patterns across sessions.
assumptions: Assumes records are stored under a stable device, account, or pseudonymous identifier, or are otherwise grouped per user.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node may differ by catalog version; this is the standard linkability-from-stored-records case.

title: Location history can identify the user or household
description: Even if direct identifiers are absent, precise home/work locations and repeated movement patterns in stored GPS traces can identify a specific individual or household when processed by the destination store or downstream analytics.
assumptions: Assumes the stored traces are sufficiently precise and persistent to permit singling out or re-identification.
uncertainty_note: Node chosen as best-fit for identifiability through quasi-identifiers and inference from location traces.

title: Sensitive information can be inferred from stored movement patterns
description: The destination store's retention of timestamped location traces enables inference of sensitive facts such as religion, health status, political affiliation, workplace, habits, or intimate relationships based on visits and co-location patterns.
assumptions: Assumes the store retains enough historical detail for profiling or downstream analysis.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id may vary; threat is classic detectability/inference of sensitive states from location history.

title: Users may be unaware that detailed location history is retained
description: If the app writes GPS traces with timestamps to persistent storage without clear, timely notice, users may not understand that their movements are being continuously recorded and retained, undermining transparency.
assumptions: Assumes notice in the UI/privacy information is incomplete, delayed, or not sufficiently specific about persistence and granularity.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit unawareness node; exact numbering may differ by LINDDUN Pro release.

title: Retention of detailed location history may violate data minimization or purpose limitation
description: Persistently storing precise GPS traces with timestamps may be non-compliant if the system lacks a lawful basis, stores more detail than necessary, or retains the data longer than justified for the stated purpose.
assumptions: Assumes regulatory obligations such as GDPR-like minimization, purpose limitation, storage limitation, or consent requirements apply.
uncertainty_note: Compliance assessment depends on jurisdiction, stated purpose, and implemented retention/consent controls.

title: Data in transit discloses highly sensitive location and temporal metadata
description: While the flow is in transit, the payload itself contains precise coordinates and timestamps. Interception or unnecessary propagation of this flow would disclose highly sensitive movement history, and even metadata about repeated uploads can reveal behavioral patterns.
assumptions: Assumes the transmission crosses a trust boundary or could be observed by intermediaries/logging components.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit node for disclosure during transfer; exact node id may vary.

title: Excessive disclosure of longitudinal health logs to analytics
description: The data store discloses calorie, weight, and exercise logs across sessions to the analytics service. Because these are sensitive health-related data and longitudinal records, sharing the full history may exceed what is strictly necessary for the stated analysis, creating avoidable disclosure through over-broad data access.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics task could be fulfilled with a reduced time window, aggregation, or pseudonymised features rather than full raw logs.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality structure; exact subnode may vary by catalog version.

title: Linkability through cross-session aggregation of health logs
description: The analytics service reads logs across sessions for the same individual, enabling records from different times and activities to be linked into a single longitudinal profile. This can increase the ability to correlate behavior, weight changes, and exercise patterns beyond what users may expect.
assumptions: Assumes P3 can associate multiple sessions with the same person or persistent pseudonym.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; threat applicability is strong because the flow explicitly states cross-session analysis.

title: Identifiability from detailed health and activity records
description: Detailed calorie, weight, and exercise logs received by the analytics service may identify a person directly or indirectly, especially when combined over time. Even if explicit identifiers are absent from the flow description, unique longitudinal patterns can make individuals distinguishable.
assumptions: Assumes P3 has access to persistent account, device, or pseudonymous identifiers, or that behavioral uniqueness is sufficient for singling out users.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; identifiability depends on whether identifiers or highly unique patterns are available to P3.

title: Inference of sensitive health conditions from combined logs
description: By analyzing calorie, weight, and exercise logs across sessions, the analytics service can derive or infer sensitive information about a person's health condition, habits, or possible medical issues that were not explicitly provided as separate data items.
assumptions: Assumes the analysis produces or could produce condition-related conclusions from the raw logs.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the inference threat itself is strongly supported by the stated purpose of health-condition analysis.

title: Secondary use of health logs for broader analytics than expected
description: Receiving raw longitudinal health logs at the analytics service creates a risk that the data are used for analyses beyond the user's expected purpose, such as model training, profiling, or unrelated product insights, making the processing insufficiently transparent or predictable to the user.
assumptions: Assumes purpose limitation and user expectations are not tightly constrained or communicated.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; this is framed as unawareness because the flow description does not indicate whether users were informed of the full scope of analytics use.

title: Processing of sensitive health logs without valid consent or other lawful basis
description: The analytics service processes longitudinal calorie, weight, and exercise logs for health-condition analysis. Because these data can reveal health status and involve sensitive profiling, the processing may be non-compliant if explicit consent, necessity, or another valid legal basis and associated safeguards are absent or insufficient.
assumptions: Assumes the jurisdiction or policy treats these logs and derived health-condition analysis as regulated sensitive personal data.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate and legal applicability depends on jurisdiction and system context.

title: Cross-session location histories enable linkage of records and sessions
description: By querying location history across sessions, the analytics service can correlate records that were originally separated in time or context and link them into a single longitudinal profile of the same individual or household. This increases the ability to connect otherwise distinct observations.
assumptions: DS2 stores session-scoped or time-stamped location records that can be associated by persistent identifiers, device identifiers, account identifiers, or stable movement patterns.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on general LINDDUN linkage taxonomy; exact subnode may differ in your local threat tree.

title: Routine and movement patterns can identify individuals
description: Even if raw location records are pseudonymous, deriving daily routines and movement patterns can reveal home/work locations, habitual visits, and unique trajectories that make a person identifiable or re-identifiable.
assumptions: Location history contains sufficiently granular spatial-temporal data to infer distinctive patterns.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; applicability of identifiability is strong given the stated derivation of routines and patterns.

title: Analytics infers sensitive habits and behaviors from location history
description: The destination process derives new personal knowledge from historical location traces, such as daily routine, religious attendance, medical visits, workplace, social relationships, or other behavioral patterns. This creates detectability of highly sensitive facts about a person from the received data.
assumptions: Derived analytics are available to the service or downstream consumers and can expose presence at sensitive places or recurring behaviors.
uncertainty_note: Using 'D' here follows LINDDUN detectability/inference-style concerns; exact subnode may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Excessive disclosure through broad historical querying
description: The analytics service receives and processes location history across sessions to derive routines and movement patterns. If full or long-retention histories are queried when only aggregated or shorter-window data is necessary, the flow discloses more personal data than required, violating data minimization.
assumptions: The analytic purpose could be achieved with less granular, less frequent, shorter-retention, or pre-aggregated location data.

title: Secondary use of location history for behavioral profiling may be unexpected
description: Using stored location history across sessions to derive daily routines and movement patterns may go beyond the user's reasonable expectations for the original collection purpose, especially if the history was collected for operational or service-delivery reasons rather than profiling.
assumptions: The original purpose for collecting location history did not clearly include cross-session behavioral analytics.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate, but the unawareness risk is strongly supported by the stated profiling use.

title: Cross-session analytics may be incompatible with consent or stated purpose
description: If users consented only to storing or using location data for immediate service functionality, querying historical data across sessions to derive routines and movement patterns may exceed that consent or conflict with purpose limitation and proportionality requirements.
assumptions: Consent, notice, contract, or policy does not explicitly authorize longitudinal behavioral analytics on location history.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the detailed non-compliance tree.

title: Excessive disclosure of inferred health insights to the app
description: The analytics service shares inferred health-condition risk indicators, routine summaries, and trend flags with the mobile app. These outputs are sensitive inferences about the user’s health and behavior; sending more detail, granularity, or confidence information than is necessary for the app’s purpose can disclose highly sensitive personal data.
assumptions: Assumes the app does not strictly need the full fidelity of all inferred insights returned by the analytics service.
uncertainty_note: Tree node citation is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the specific Data Disclosure subtree.

title: User identification through inferred-health payloads or flow metadata
description: Even if direct identifiers are minimized, the combination of inferred health-condition risks, routine summaries, trend flags, timing, and communication metadata on this flow can enable identification or re-identification of the user, especially when correlated with other app-side knowledge.
assumptions: Assumes the payload or transport metadata is observable to components or parties beyond a strictly isolated end-to-end channel, or that the app can correlate the data with existing identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Specific Identifying subtree node is chosen by best judgment; retrieved context only provided the general Identifying definition.

title: Profiling and linkage from inferred insights
description: The analytics service’s returned insights can be linked across time and with other app-held observations to build a richer profile of the individual, and may also reveal similarity to groups with particular health conditions or routines. This creates linking risk beyond the raw source data because the inferences act as compact profile markers.
assumptions: Assumes repeated or longitudinal insight delivery and that the app or related systems can correlate these outputs with other records.
uncertainty_note: L.2.2.2 is directly supported by retrieved context for group profiling, but the individual longitudinal-linkage aspect is broader than that exact node.

title: Users may be unaware that sensitive health inferences are delivered to and exposed within the app
description: When the app receives and presents inferred risk indicators and trend flags, users may not understand that these are derived analytics rather than raw observations, what data they were based on, how accurate they are, or who can access them on the device. This undermines informed expectations and meaningful control.
assumptions: Assumes the app UX does not clearly explain the origin, meaning, confidence, and visibility of these inferred insights.
uncertainty_note: Specific Unawareness subtree node is approximate because no U-tree context was retrieved.

title: App-side exposure of sensitive inferred health data
description: Once received, the companion app may store, cache, display, or otherwise process the inferred insights in ways that expose them to unauthorized viewers on the device, other apps, backups, screenshots, or notifications. The destination’s handling therefore creates a data disclosure risk distinct from transmission.
assumptions: Assumes the mobile app may persist or surface these insights locally or through OS integrations.
uncertainty_note: Tree node citation is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the specific Data Disclosure subtree.

title: Insufficient privacy-aware cybersecurity controls for inferred health insights in the app
description: Because this flow carries sensitive inferred health information, inadequate security risk management at the mobile app—such as weak local protection, insecure notification handling, or poor access control—can create compliance issues tied to disclosure and identification risks. This is a non-compliance concern insofar as privacy-relevant security safeguards may be insufficient for the sensitivity of the data.
assumptions: Assumes applicable legal or policy obligations require stronger safeguards for sensitive health-related inferred data.
uncertainty_note: Nc should be grounded in underlying privacy threats; this entry is included because the flow clearly involves sensitive inferred health data, but exact compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and system context.

title: Sensitive inferred health-risk indicators may be over-disclosed to the user interface
description: The app sends inferred condition indicators such as eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals to the dashboard. These are special-category health inferences; presenting more detail, confidence data, or historical trend granularity than necessary can expose highly sensitive information on-screen and increase privacy harm if seen by others or surfaced in notifications/screenshots.
assumptions: The dashboard may show detailed risk labels, trends, or confidence values rather than a minimal, privacy-preserving summary.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the detailed threat tree for Data Disclosure.

title: Interception of dashboard data in transit could disclose sensitive health inferences
description: The flow carries trends and inferred eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals from the mobile app process to the user-facing endpoint. If this transmission is observable in transit, sensitive health-related content could be disclosed to unauthorized parties.
assumptions: The rendering path may traverse device IPC, local network sync, push/update channels, or other transport mechanisms that are not fully protected end-to-end.
uncertainty_note: For an on-device app-to-user display flow, 'in transit' exposure may be limited; included because LINDDUN allows flow-level disclosure threats where data can be observed during delivery.

title: User may be unaware that the dashboard presents inferred, not directly observed, health conditions
description: By displaying condition indicators and trends, the app may cause the wearer to believe the information is factual diagnosis rather than probabilistic inference. If the app does not clearly explain the source, confidence, limitations, and intended use of these indicators, the user lacks awareness about how sensitive conclusions about them are being generated and communicated.
assumptions: The UI may not clearly distinguish raw measurements from inferred risk signals or explain model limitations.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate because the retrieved context did not provide the detailed Unawareness subtree.

title: Recipient may be unaware of onward exposure risks from viewing sensitive indicators
description: Once the user receives the dashboard output, they may not realize that the displayed health inferences can be exposed through shoulder surfing, lock-screen previews, screenshots, screen recording, or sharing with others. Lack of contextual warning or privacy controls reduces awareness of the consequences of receiving this information in visible form.
assumptions: The app may not provide privacy notices, discreet display modes, or warnings before showing sensitive indicators.
uncertainty_note: Destination-side unawareness is inferred from the visible-display nature of the flow; exact subtree citation is approximate.

title: Displaying inferred health-risk signals may create non-compliance if transparency and special-category-data obligations are unmet
description: Eating-disorder and diabetes risk indicators are health-related inferences that can trigger heightened legal and policy obligations. If the app presents these indicators without adequate transparency, lawful basis/consent where required, data minimization, appropriate safeguards, or user rights support, this flow may contribute to non-compliance.
assumptions: Applicable law or policy treats inferred health-risk indicators as sensitive or special-category personal data.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on jurisdiction and product context; included because the flow clearly involves sensitive health inferences.

title: Excessive disclosure of full health and location dataset to third-party cloud provider
description: The Health Analytics Service shares the full health and location dataset, along with analytics data and models, with a third-party cloud provider for hosting and replication. Sending the full dataset to an external party may disclose more personal data than is strictly necessary for the hosting purpose, especially given the sensitivity of health and location data.
assumptions: Assumes the cloud provider is a separate third party and that not all raw health and location data are strictly required in identifiable form for hosting/replication.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement for unnecessary/excessive disclosure; exact sub-node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Third-party cloud storage and replication expose sensitive data to additional parties and contexts
description: Upon receipt, the cloud hosting provider stores and replicates analytics data, models, and the full health and location dataset. This creates disclosure risk because sensitive personal data become accessible within the provider's operational environment, backups, and replication infrastructure, potentially beyond the original intended processing context.
assumptions: Assumes provider-side storage, backup, replication, or administrative access can expose data to personnel, subprocessors, or jurisdictions beyond the primary analytics service.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree sub-node for recipient-side onward disclosure/storage may differ across LINDDUN Pro materials.

title: Identifiability from transmission of full health and location dataset
description: The data flow contains the full health and location dataset. Even if direct identifiers were reduced elsewhere, the combination of detailed health and location attributes in transit can make individuals directly or indirectly identifiable.
assumptions: Assumes the dataset includes sufficiently granular health and location attributes to single out or re-identify individuals.
uncertainty_note: Sub-node chosen by best judgement for identifiability through data content in transit.

title: Linkability of records across analytics, models, health, and location data
description: Combining analytics data, models, and the full health and location dataset in one transfer can enable linking records about the same person across multiple data domains. This may allow the cloud provider or anyone with access to the flow to correlate behavior, health status, and movement patterns.
assumptions: Assumes common identifiers, quasi-identifiers, or stable patterns exist across the transferred datasets or model artifacts.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node may vary; threat is grounded in cross-dataset correlation/linkability.

title: Cloud provider can infer sensitive user profiles from hosted datasets and models
description: By hosting the full health and location dataset together with analytics artifacts and models, the cloud provider may be able to infer sensitive characteristics, behaviors, or future risks about individuals beyond what was explicitly disclosed in any single record.
assumptions: Assumes the provider has technical or administrative access to stored data or model artifacts sufficient to derive additional insights.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree sub-node selected by best judgement for inference from available data and models.

description: Users may not reasonably expect their full health and location dataset to be hosted and replicated by a third-party cloud provider, particularly across multiple regions or backup systems. If this external hosting and replication are not clearly communicated and covered by an appropriate legal basis or consent, the flow creates a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes transparency notices, contracts, or consent/legal basis may not explicitly cover third-party hosting and replication of full sensitive datasets.
